## Becoming A Test Pilot Once Every Year by Jim Trusty

Is it time for an annual inspection? Ever dream of being a Test Pilot?

Four strangers to my aircraft checked, filled , turned, tightened touched, replaced, repaired, removed, looked, pondered, and evaluated over 100 items on a factory inspection checklist and then complied with the latest Airworthiness Directives from problems encountered in the last year or SO with its make and model. Two of   these young men were A&P trainees with absolutely no experience as mechanics .

The first flight after the annual inspection of your airplane can either be totally uneventful or a very flight. have known and trusted my mechanic for years, and he seldom misses anything. This is be cause live , happy and satisfied pilotlcustomers can recommend you to others and then return the next time to spend more money Even SO, you should always expect the worst and be prepared. Just think about this statement while use my case as an example. busy good

Some that fellow pilots have experienced over the years as but are not limited to, the following: engine oil not refilled, rags left in gear connected, spark plugs left out on one side , screws not replaced in cowling cover; brakes not bled, fuel turned off, hydraulic fluid not refilled; gear handle in the UP position while the gear is actually DOWN; and tools left on the enthings they gine; in the floor under the cabin; and under the seats and carpets.

If tell you about a problem search and that think the problem was caught just in time; then you have been forewarned to watch that area much more closely than you normally would. Some would argue that the A&P should be required to fly the air craft before release it back to the owner and even others would say that makes as much sense as having the owner participate in the actual work of doing the annual inspection. might also add that no pilots were injured, crashed , or died be cause of the foregoing list of mistakes. And in testimony to the hard work that our mechanics do, really feel that it is impossible to do what do and combine that with what we do to the airplane during the year and not have an adventure occasionally. But we should be apprehensive. RIGHT? they

As a flight instructor who does an awful lot of proficiency training, flight reviews, and transition work on complex/high  performance aircraft, have found that pilots who DO NOT fly on regular basis are generally not as ready as should be to react to an "unexpected happening in the air. When review emergency procedures (such as gear; radio, and vacuum failures and add fuel transfer mistakes) find that most are not as well versed in recovery procedures as should be. they pilots they This is clearly the fault of the pilot. We get a little complacent and start comparing flying with driving and mistakenly think if something goes wrong that we will have plenty of time to just pull over to the side of the sky and call WRONG! never cease to be amazed when read ing accident reports from the NTSB and others just how much of a role pilots often play in what happened and how with just a normal amount of spe cific training the entire thing could have turned out differently:

Careful selection of mechanic based on known skill levels for your particular aircraft will not keep something from happening, but it certainly couldn't hurt. Do not make the mistake many pilots make of mechanic selection based on the cost of the annual. This is certainly inviting trouble. Bring a squawk list with you and explain the items included. Work with them; especially since it is to your benefit. solely

The list of people hurt andlor killed in aviation accidents does not have to include your name You really have a choice in this decision. Is it time for an annual inspection? Ever dream of being a Test Pilot? Let's be careful up there.

Jim Trusty was the FAA/Aviation Industry National Flight Instructor of the Year (1997) and still works full-time as pilotlflight instructor at MQY in Tennessee
